title: Evolution and Revolution in Artificial Intelligence in Education
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
extended_summary:
This paper is a historical and forward-looking position piece on the field of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED), rather than an empirical study of a specific intervention. The authors ask what the field’s strengths have been over the previous 25 years and what directions it should take to remain relevant as education changes.

To answer this, the paper analyzes 47 papers published in the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education across three benchmark years (1994, 2004, and 2014). The analysis codes papers by type, domain, breadth, interaction style, collaborative structure, technology, setting, and learning goals, with a particular focus on how AIED has emphasized student use of computers in formal school settings, often in STEM, step-based problem-solving contexts.

The paper argues that AIED has made strong progress in improving tutoring systems and evaluation rigor, but also that the field remains too narrow. It proposes two parallel directions: an evolutionary path that refines existing classroom-centered work in collaboration with teachers, and a revolutionary path that embeds intelligent learning environments into learners’ everyday lives, supports broader skills and contexts, and expands beyond stand-alone computer-based tutoring. The paper concludes that future AIED research should diversify technologies, domains, settings, and stakeholders, including stronger integration with classroom practice, culture, informal learning, and teacher collaboration.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is an adaptive educational software environment that provides individualized instruction, hints, feedback, and support based on learner responses and models of learner knowledge.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a historical/review analysis of AI in education papers and discusses ITS/ILE research trends rather than evaluating a single system; it references intelligent tutoring systems broadly as the dominant class of tools in the field.

findings.finding_summary: Across 47 IJAIED papers from 1994, 2004, and 2014, the authors report a shift toward more empirical work, greater breadth of topics, more collaboration support, and stronger learning goals beyond domain knowledge. They characterize this as evidence that ITS/ILE research has become more rigorous and more classroom-relevant over time, but no single causal effect size is reported because this is a review synthesis.
findings.measure: Review coding of 47 papers by empirical status, domain, interaction style, collaborative structure, and learning goals

quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative historical review of IJAIED papers, not a primary evaluation of one tool with causal identification. The paper synthesizes trends descriptively and does not report experimental estimates for a specific system.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ITS/ILE research is becoming more rigorous and broader in scope, which is potentially important at the field level. However, it does not provide a measurable effect estimate for a tool, so impact on student outcomes cannot be quantified from this paper.
